common_name: UpTick Gold Coreopsis (Solid Golden-Yellow Large-Flowered Tickseed)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; UpTick Gold is the solid-color, clear golden-yellow member of the vegetatively propagated UpTick series.

directions: UpTick Gold produces unusually large, up to three-inch, unmarked golden-yellow flowers in dense succession on a compact, mounded plant, giving it a cleaner, single-color look than the bicolor UpTick siblings bred alongside it. Because it is sterile it channels its energy into nonstop flowering from late spring through hard frost rather than seed set, and it needs no deadheading to keep performing. Site it in lean to average, sharply drained soil in full sun, since crowns are prone to winter rot in heavy, wet ground. A light midseason shearing refreshes the habit if plants start to sprawl in rich soil.

common_name: UpTick Cream Coreopsis (Pale Butter-Yellow Large-Flowered Tickseed)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; UpTick Cream carries the softest, palest flower color of the UpTick series, useful for toning down hot-colored plantings.

directions: UpTick Cream softens the usual tickseed color palette with large, pale butter-yellow flowers that read almost ivory in bright sun, a gentler tone than the saturated golds typical of the genus. Like its series-mates it is a sterile, vegetatively propagated selection that blooms continuously from spring into fall without setting seed or requiring deadheading. Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, where the compact, densely branched habit stays tidy without staking. It pairs well at the front of a border with blue- or purple-flowered companions that would clash with brighter yellow coreopsis.

common_name: UpTick Red Coreopsis (Solid Deep Red Large-Flowered Tickseed)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; UpTick Red is a nearly solid deep-red-flowered selection, an unusually saturated color for a large-flowered coreopsis.

directions: UpTick Red breaks from the yellow-and-gold color range that dominates Coreopsis grandiflora, opening large flowers in a deep brick-red that only narrowly rims to gold at the very base of each petal. The dense, compact mound blooms without interruption from late spring through frost and, being sterile, never diverts energy into seed production. Grow in full sun in lean, sharply drained soil, and avoid overly rich ground, which can cause floppy growth. Its strong color makes it a useful accent among the more typical gold-toned coreopsis in a mixed planting.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: UpTick Yellow & Red Coreopsis (Bicolor Gold-Tipped Red Large-Flowered Tickseed)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; UpTick Yellow & Red combines a red petal base with bright gold petal tips on the same large-flowered, compact plant as the rest of the series.

directions: UpTick Yellow & Red carries a sharp two-tone flower, a wine-red inner band giving way to bright golden petal tips, so each three-inch bloom reads as distinctly bicolor rather than the softer eye-zone patterning seen in some other coreopsis cultivars. The compact, well-branched plant flowers non-stop from late spring to hard frost and needs no deadheading to keep cycling through new buds. Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, the same conditions wild Coreopsis grandiflora favors, and expect strong heat and drought tolerance once established. Its bold contrast makes it a good anchor color for pollinator plantings that mix warm-toned perennials.

common_name: UpTick Coral Red Coreopsis (Bicolor Coral-and-Gold Large-Flowered Tickseed)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; UpTick Coral Red shows a softer coral-red tone than UpTick Red, fading toward gold at the petal tips.

directions: UpTick Coral Red opens in a warm coral-red that softens toward the gold petal tips, a gentler, more blended coloring than the sharper red-and-gold contrast of its Yellow & Red series-mate. Flowering is continuous from late spring through frost on a dense, compact mound that rarely needs deadheading or staking. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, and expect the same reliable heat and drought tolerance shared across the sterile, vegetatively propagated UpTick line. It blends easily with both hot and pastel color schemes given its intermediate coral tone.

common_name: Cosmic Eye Coreopsis (Big Bang Series Gold Tickseed with Deep Red Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Cosmic Eye is a patented multi-species Big Bang series hybrid bred by Darrell Probst and, like its Redshift and Star Cluster series-mates already in this dataset, sets no viable seed.

directions: Cosmic Eye carries a bold, wide burgundy-red ring around a small gold button center, with the outer two-thirds of each petal finishing in clear golden yellow, giving the bloom a stronger, more concentrated eye pattern than the thinner red banding seen on Redshift. Flower stems branch freely above a full clump, keeping the plant in bloom from early summer to fall frost without any seed drain since the hybrid is sterile. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil and expect strong drought tolerance once roots are established. Cut back by roughly a third after the first flush to keep the clump full and encourage continued branching.

common_name: Lightning Bug Threadleaf Coreopsis (Glowing Chartreuse-Gold Tickseed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Lightning Bug is a threadleaf coreopsis selected for unusually bright, glowing chartreuse-gold flower color.

directions: Lightning Bug produces flowers in a bright, glowing chartreuse-gold that reads noticeably cooler and more luminous in low light than the warmer clear yellow of Zagreb or Moonbeam, making it stand out at dusk or in a partly shaded border edge. It forms a dense, rounded mound of the fine, needle-like foliage typical of threadleaf coreopsis and blooms heavily from early summer into fall. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, where it tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil with ease once established. Shear back by about a third after the first flush to renew a tidy shape and prompt continued bloom.

common_name: Sweet Marmalade Threadleaf Coreopsis (Golden-Orange Fine-Textured Tickseed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Sweet Marmalade is a Proven Winners threadleaf coreopsis bred for warm, marmalade-toned golden-orange flowers on a compact, rounded plant.

directions: Sweet Marmalade opens in a warm, marmalade-orange gold that deepens slightly toward the center, a richer tone than the clear lemon-yellow of Moonbeam and closer in feel to the fiery Sizzle & Spice cultivars already in this dataset, though less intensely red. The compact, well-branched mound of fine, airy foliage stays dense and self-supporting through a long summer bloom season. Plant in full sun in lean to average, well-drained soil, since this species performs poorly in heavy, wet clay over winter. Deadheading is not required for rebloom, but a light midseason shearing keeps the habit tight in richer soil.

common_name: License to Chill Sky Blue Coreopsis (Novel Lavender-Blue Tickseed)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Sky Blue is a Walters Gardens hybrid bred for a lavender-blue flower color previously unknown in the genus Coreopsis.

directions: Sky Blue is bred from interspecific coreopsis crosses to produce a soft lavender-blue flower color that had never before existed in the genus, a striking departure from the yellow, pink, and red tones of every other cultivar in this dataset. The low, compact mound of narrow foliage stays tidy without staking and flowers over a long summer season, holding its cool color best in regions with moderate summer nights. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, and avoid heavy, poorly drained ground where crowns are prone to winter rot. Its unusual color makes it a useful bridging plant between blue- and gold-toned perennial plantings.

common_name: License to Chill Frozen Lemonade Coreopsis (Pale Ivory-Yellow Compact Tickseed)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Frozen Lemonade is a Walters Gardens License to Chill series-mate to Sky Blue, bred for a pale, icy ivory-yellow flower color and the same compact habit.

directions: Frozen Lemonade carries the same low, dense, well-behaved habit as its Sky Blue series-mate but in a pale, icy ivory-yellow flower color, softer and cooler than the warm golds typical of grandiflora and verticillata cultivars in this dataset. It stays compact without staking and blooms steadily through summer into fall on a full, rounded mound of narrow foliage. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, since this hybrid line declines quickly in soggy, poorly drained ground over winter. Its pale color works well softening hot-colored perennial combinations or paired with its own blue and purple series-mates.

common_name: Goldquelle Cutleaf Coneflower (Compact Double-Flowered Golden Rudbeckia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, average to rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Goldquelle (German for 'gold fountain') is a compact, fully double-flowered cutleaf coneflower cultivar, much shorter than the double heirloom Hortensia and the tall single Herbstsonne already in this dataset.

directions: Goldquelle stays a compact 2 to 2.5 feet tall, far shorter than the 5-to-8-foot species and the towering Hortensia and Herbstsonne cultivars already in this dataset, making it a better fit for a mid-border position where a full-size cutleaf coneflower would overwhelm the space. Its fully double, golden-yellow flowers form neat globe-shaped pompoms rather than the flatter, more open blooms of the wild species, held on sturdy stems above dark green, deeply cut foliage from midsummer into fall. Grow in moist, average to rich soil in full sun to partial shade, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor. Unlike the rhizomatous Hortensia, Goldquelle spreads more slowly and stays better behaved in a mixed perennial bed.

common_name: Becky Mixed Black-Eyed Susan (Dwarf Bedding Rudbeckia Color Mix)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow once soil has warmed; Becky Mixed is a dwarf, uniform seed series bred for early, heavy bloom in containers and bedding rows in a mix of gold, mahogany, and bicolor tones.

directions: Becky Mixed is a dwarf, densely branching seed series bred for uniform, early flowering in a color mix spanning solid gold, mahogany-red, and gold-and-mahogany bicolors, all on plants under 14 inches tall that need no staking. Its compact size and heavy bud count make it especially well suited to containers, window boxes, and the front of bedding rows, unlike the taller, looser habit of open-pollinated hirta strains. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun; plants germinate and flower quickly, typically blooming within ten weeks of sowing. Deadhead regularly to keep the display going through summer heat and to prevent the mix from going quickly to seed.

common_name: Becky Cinnamon Bicolor Black-Eyed Susan (Dwarf Mahogany-and-Gold Rudbeckia)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow once soil has warmed; Cinnamon Bicolor is a single-color selection from the dwarf Becky series, bred for a consistent mahogany-red and gold bicolor bloom rather than the full mixed-color strain.

directions: Cinnamon Bicolor was separated out from the wider Becky Mixed strain to offer a consistent, uniform flower color: a deep mahogany-red inner zone giving way to a bright gold outer band on every bloom, rather than the random assortment of solids and bicolors in the full mix. Plants stay compact and self-supporting under 14 inches tall with heavy bud counts, making the strain useful where a predictable, coordinated color is wanted in containers or bedding rows. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, where seed-grown plants germinate and flower quickly, typically within ten weeks of sowing. Deadhead through the season to sustain bloom into fall as summer heat builds.
